mainTopic: Finishing מחזרת (an animal turning its head to eat), then animals that jump or fall and cause damage, and the rule of תחלתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס
overview: The amud opens by finishing the argument between רב and שמואל about מחזרת, an animal that turns its head to eat produce at the side of the road. The גמרא shows that each of them has his own reason for this case that does not depend on the rule of בור ברשותו. It then suggests that a ברייתא with רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי already holds this same argument. It rejects that idea: the תנאים are really arguing about the verse 'ובער בשדה אחר', and in the end about the case of אילפא and רבי אושעיא. Next comes a new משנה about a dog or goat that jumps off a roof and breaks vessels, and a dog that sets a grain stack on fire with a burning cake. From the word 'jumped', the גמרא infers that a case which starts with carelessness and ends in an accident is exempt. It then defends the opposing view and discusses when even a fall makes the owner pay, as with a narrow wall. The amud ends with a ברייתא that sorts jumping damage by direction and by who jumped.

steps.title: רב's own reason: you can't put produce by the road and blame my ox
steps.stepSummary: רב can hold the usual rule that a בור ברשותו is exempt. The case of produce is different for its own reason: the animal's owner can say, 'You can't put your produce near the public road and then make my ox pay for it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Generally, a pit in one's own domain is exempt. But here it is different, because the animal's owner can say: 'It is not in your power to bring your produce close to the public domain and then make my oxen liable for it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רב's ruling (pay only for the benefit) has its own reason. It does not come from the general rule about pits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general law of בור ברשותו is set aside. רב's real reason is that the produce owner is partly at fault for placing his produce so close to where animals walk. Because of that, he cannot collect full damages from the animal's owner.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit or obstacle that a person made in his own property
It is not in your power, you can't have it both ways

phrases.english: Generally, a pit in his own domain is exempt;
but here it is different, because he can say:
phrases.notes: The one speaking is the owner of the animal, talking to the owner of the produce.

phrases.english: It is not all in your power
to bring your produce close to the public domain,
and also to hold my oxen liable for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשָׁאנֵי הָכָא, דְּאָמַר: לָאו כֹּל כְּמִינָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues from before this section, defending רב's view of מחזרת without tying it to בור ברשותו.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Independent reason (סברא) specific to this case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think רב's ruling depends on the general law of בור ברשותו.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב can hold בור ברשותו פטור. His ruling on מחזרת comes from the produce owner's own fault in placing produce near the road.

steps.title: שמואל's own reason: the animal can see the produce
steps.stepSummary: שמואל can hold that a בור ברשותו is liable. A pit is something a person might not notice, but produce is something the animal plainly sees, so its owner pays the full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל can say: generally, a pit in one's own domain is liable. Granted, with a pit you can say the one who got hurt was not aware of it. But with produce, can you say the animal was not aware? It sees it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives שמואל's side. His ruling (pay the full damage) also rests on a reason that fits this case specifically.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit is hidden, so it makes sense to blame the one who made it. Produce is out in the open and the animal sees it, so eating it is the animal's own act, and its owner pays for the full damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it makes sense in one case (but not in the other)
Not on his mind, he was not aware

phrases.english: And Shmuel can say:
Generally, a pit in his own domain is liable;

phrases.aramaic: דְּבִשְׁלָמָא בּוֹר, אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר לָאו אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ;
phrases.english: for granted, with a pit, one can say he was not aware of it;
phrases.notes: "He" is the one who fell in and got hurt. He didn't realize a pit was there.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא פֵּירוֹת, מִי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר לָאו אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ?!
phrases.english: but with produce, can one say it was not aware of it?!
Why, it sees them!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבִשְׁלָמָא בּוֹר, אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר לָאו אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to step 1, giving שמואל's independent reason.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Independent reason (סברא) specific to this case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think שמואל's ruling depends on the general law of בור ברשותו.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל's ruling on מחזרת rests on the fact that the animal sees the produce, unlike a hidden pit.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רב and שמואל are shown to have their own reasons for מחזרת. Their argument is not really about the general rule of בור ברשותו.

steps.title: Suggesting the argument already appears between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the argument about מחזרת is already found in a ברייתא. There, רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה split between eating from the middle of the square and eating from its sides, and רבי יוסי and רבי אלעזר say an animal's way is to walk, not to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that מחזרת is an argument of תנאים? For it was taught: If the animal ate from the middle of the square, the owner pays for the benefit; if from the sides of the square, he pays for the damage. These are the words of רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה. רבי יוסי and רבי אלעזר say: It is not an animal's way to eat, only to walk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests that the רב and שמואל argument may already be an argument in a ברייתא. This sets up the next steps, where the גמרא tries to read the ברייתא carefully.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plan is to match רב and שמואל to two sides of an older argument. רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה give a rule for the middle and for the sides. רבי יוסי says eating is not an animal's usual way at all, and the גמרא now needs to work out where exactly he disagrees.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that turns its head to eat
It is an argument between תנאים
What the animal benefited (the value of the food to it)

phrases.english: Shall we say that the case of a turning animal is a dispute of tanna'im?
For it was taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: אָכְלָה מִתּוֹךְ הָרְחָבָה – מְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁנֶּהֱנֵית,
phrases.english: If it ate from the middle of the square, it pays for what it benefited;
from the sides of the square, it pays for what it damaged;
these are the words of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar say:
It is not its way to eat, but only to walk.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining each אמורא's reasoning, the גמרא looks for an earlier argument between תנאים that matches.
steps.raayaObject: That the argument of רב and שמואל about מחזרת is an older argument between תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה against רבי יוסי and רבי אלעזר

steps.title: רבי יוסי seems to say the same as the תנא קמא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out a problem: if רבי יוסי is talking about the sides of the square, he says exactly what the תנא קמא said, that the owner pays for the damage. So what are they arguing about?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי is the same as the תנא קמא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the simple reading of the ברייתא. It looks like רבי יוסי adds nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא already ruled that eating from the sides of the square means paying the full damage. If רבי יוסי also means full damage for the sides, there is no argument, and a ברייתא would not present two views for no reason.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed or first-quoted opinion in a ברייתא or משנה

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei is the same as the first tanna!
phrases.notes: The first opinion here is רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a difficulty with how to read the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of רבי יוסי's view in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both opinions give full damage for eating at the sides of the square, there is no real argument between them.

steps.title: They argue about an animal that turns its head
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי argue about מחזרת. The תנא קמא says the owner pays only for the benefit, and רבי יוסי says he pays for the full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the difference between them is a turning animal. The תנא קמא holds that for a turning animal too, he pays for the benefit. רבי יוסי holds it pays for the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the difficulty by finding the exact case they argue about: an animal that turns its head to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the ברייתא has a real argument, and it is the same as the argument between רב and שמואל. The תנא קמא's view (benefit only) lines up with רב, and רבי יוסי's view (full damage) lines up with שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them

phrases.english: Rather, the difference between them is a turning animal:
The first tanna holds:
for a turning animal too, he pays for what it benefited;

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי סָבַר: מְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁהִזִּיקָה.
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yosei holds: it pays for what it damaged.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 4 by finding the case where they argue.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finding the specific case of the argument (מאי בינייהו)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוסי seemed to repeat the תנא קמא's ruling for the sides of the square.
steps.terutzMaskana: They argue about מחזרת: the תנא קמא says benefit only, and רבי יוסי says full damage. This matches the argument of רב and שמואל.
steps.whatToRemember: For now, the ברייתא is read as an argument about מחזרת: the תנא קמא matches רב (pays for the benefit), and רבי יוסי matches שמואל (pays the full damage). The next step rejects this reading.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this reading held, the argument between רב and שמואל would already be an argument between תנאים. The next step rejects this and says both sides agree about מחזרת.

steps.title: Everyone agrees about מחזרת; the argument is about the verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 3. Both sides of the ברייתא agree about מחזרת. They argue about what the words 'ובער בשדה אחר' leave out. One side says the public domain is left out. רבי יוסי says only the damager's own property is left out.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees about an animal that turns its head, either like רב or like שמואל. Here they argue about 'and it consumed in another's field.' One Sage holds: 'in another's field,' and not in the public domain. The other Sage holds: 'in another's field,' and not in the damager's domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the claim that the ברייתא is arguing about מחזרת. It gives a different topic for the argument: how to read the verse 'ובער בשדה אחר'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 4-5 said the תנא קמא and רבי יוסי argue about מחזרת. Now the גמרא says they agree on מחזרת and instead read the verse differently. The first side says the verse leaves out the public domain, so the owner is exempt there. רבי יוסי says it leaves out only the damager's property, so the owner is liable even in the public domain.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it consumed in another's field' (שמות 22:4), the source for liability when an animal eats
The property of the one whose animal did the damage

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides learn an exemption from the same words 'ובער בשדה אחר'. The only question is which place the verse leaves out.

phrases.english: No; everyone agrees about an animal that turns its head –
either like רב or like שמואל.
phrases.notes: Whichever way the הלכה goes on מחזרת, both sides of the ברייתא hold the same view about it.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכָא בְּ״בִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ קָא מִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: And here they argue about 'it consumed in another's field' –
One Sage holds: 'and it consumed in another's field'
– and not in the public domain;
and the other Sage holds: 'and it consumed in another's field'
– and not in the damager's domain.
phrases.notes: This is רבי יוסי's side, so for him the owner pays even when the animal ate in the public domain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading from step 5 that the argument is about מחזרת.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the ברייתא is a source for the רב/שמואל argument about מחזרת.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be explained as an argument about how to read the verse, with both sides agreeing on מחזרת.

steps.title: Why would a verse be needed to exempt eating on the damager's property?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוסי's reading. Of course the owner is exempt when the animal eats on his own property. He can simply say, 'What is your produce doing on my land?'
steps.simpleTranslation: In the damager's domain? Let him say: 'What is your produce doing on my property?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the verse would need to teach that the owner is exempt on his own property. That seems obvious without any verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner is plainly not responsible for produce someone else left on his land without permission. So reading 'ובער בשדה אחר' as leaving out the damager's property makes the verse teach nothing new. That puts step 6's way of explaining רבי יוסי in doubt.

phrases.english: In the damager's domain? –
Let him say: what is your produce doing on my property?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the second reading of the verse given in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'ובער בשדה אחר' comes to leave out the damager's own property.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That exemption is obvious from common sense, so no verse is needed for it.

steps.title: The difference is the rulings of אילפא and רבי אושעיא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes its answer. The two sides of the ברייתא actually differ over the earlier rulings of אילפא and רבי אושעיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the argument between אילפא and רבי אושעיא is the difference between them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the explanation it gave in step 6. It says the real practical difference between the sides is a pair of rulings that came up earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אילפא and רבי אושעיא each gave an earlier ruling about an animal in the public domain. אילפא spoke of one that stretches its neck and eats off another animal's back, and רבי אושעיא of one that leaps and eats out of a basket. Both said the owner pays. The first side in the ברייתא would exempt the owner, since every kind of eating in the public domain is exempt. רבי יוסי would make him pay, treating it like eating from the victim's own property.

phrases.english: Rather, the argument of אילפא and רבי אושעיא
is the difference between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דְּאִילְפָא וְרַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by changing what the argument is about.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the practical difference between the two sides
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference was whether the verse leaves out the damager's own property.
steps.terutzMaskana: The difference is the case of אילפא and רבי אושעיא, where an animal eats off another animal's back in the public domain.
steps.whatToRemember: In the end, the ברייתא is not a source for the argument about מחזרת. Its two sides differ over the case of אילפא and רבי אושעיא.

steps.title: A dog or goat that jumped from a roof
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה. If a dog or a goat jumps off a roof and breaks vessels, the owner pays full damage, because these animals are known to jump.
steps.simpleTranslation: A dog or a goat that jumped from a rooftop and broke vessels: the owner pays full damage, because they are מועדין.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins here. It rules that the owner pays full damage when his jumping dog or goat breaks things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jumping is normal behavior for these animals, so they count as מועד for it. That is why the owner pays full damage, not half.

keyTerms.meaning: Known or expected to do this, so the owner pays fully

phrases.english: MISHNA:
A dog or a goat

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁקָּפְצוּ מֵרֹאשׁ הַגָּג, וְשָׁבְרוּ אֶת הַכֵּלִים –
phrases.english: that jumped from a rooftop and broke the vessels –

phrases.aramaic: מְשַׁלֵּם נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהֵן מוּעָדִין.
phrases.english: he pays full damage, because they are forewarned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals that jump and break vessels make their owner pay full damage, because they are מועדין for jumping.

steps.title: The dog that took a burning cake to a grain stack
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues. A dog took a cake off the coals and brought it to a grain stack. It ate the cake and set the stack on fire. The owner pays full damage for the cake and half damage for the stack.
steps.simpleTranslation: A dog that took a cake and went to a stack, ate the cake and set fire to the stack: for the cake he pays full damage, and for the stack he pays half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case where one act of a dog causes two different damages, each paid in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating the cake is ordinary eating, so the owner pays in full. The fire in the stack is paid at only half. The משנה does not say why here.

keyTerms.meaning: A cake baked right on the coals

phrases.english: A dog that took a cake and went to a stack of grain,
ate the cake and set fire to the stack –
for the cake he pays full damage,
and for the stack he pays half damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second case of the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Full damage for the cake that was eaten; half damage for the stack that was set on fire.

steps.title: Jumped, not fell: careless start, accidental end is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the משנה closely. The owner pays because the animals jumped. If they had fallen, he would be exempt. So the תנא holds that תחלתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that they jumped. But if they fell, he is exempt. So he holds: if it began through carelessness and ended by accident, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a rule from the word 'jumped' in the משנה. This sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Letting the animals get onto the roof was already careless. Still, the משנה makes the owner pay only when they jumped. That suggests he is exempt when they fell by accident. So the תנא seems to hold that carelessness at the start does not make you pay for an accident at the end.

keyTerms.meaning: It began through carelessness and ended by accident

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה never mentions falling. The exemption for falling is the גמרא's own inference from the word 'jumped'.
steps.whyThisMatters: תחלתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס is a major rule in the laws of damages and guardians, and here the גמרא ties it to this משנה.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The reason is that they jumped,
but if they fell – he is exempt;
apparently he holds:
if it began with carelessness and ended by accident – he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a rule from the wording of the first case of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: The view that תחלתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס is exempt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's wording 'שקפצו' (they jumped), which implies that falling is exempt.

steps.title: A ברייתא backs up the reading of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says openly what the גמרא read into the משנה: if they jumped, the owner pays full damage, and if they fell, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is also taught in a ברייתא: a dog or a goat jumped from the top of a roof and broke vessels. The owner pays full damage. If they fell, the owners are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports the reading it just made of the משנה in Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 11 the גמרא only inferred that a fall is exempt. Here a ברייתא says it outright, 'נפלו פטורין'. That backs up the idea that this תנא exempts a case that starts with carelessness and ends in an accident.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way (a ברייתא that supports what was just said)
They jumped (on purpose, as these animals tend to do)

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
A dog or a goat that jumped from the top of the roof
and broke the vessels:
he pays full damage.
If they fell, they are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the inference made in Step 11 with an explicit ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The view that a case starting with carelessness and ending in an accident is exempt
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating that animals who fell from a roof are exempt

steps.title: A problem for the view that holds the owner liable
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא fits the view that a careless start with an accidental end is exempt. What will the view that says 'liable' do with it?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says that if it starts with carelessness and ends in an accident, he is exempt. But for the one who says he is liable, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the ברייתא into a challenge against the opposite opinion, the one that holds the owner liable in such cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Letting the animals up on the roof was careless, because they might jump. The fall itself was an accident. So the ברייתא's exemption seems to prove that this mixed case is exempt, which goes against the view that says 'חייב'.

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well for the one who says…
It starts with carelessness and ends in an accident
What is there to say? (how will he explain it?)

phrases.english: This works well for the one who says:
if it starts with carelessness and ends in an accident, he is exempt,
but for the one who says he is liable,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא from Step 12 to attack the opposing view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a case that starts with carelessness and ends in an accident is liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא exempts animals that fell from the roof even though letting them up there was careless. That looks like a mixed case ruled exempt.

steps.title: The vessels were right next to the wall
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about vessels placed close to the wall. A normal jump would clear them, so there was no carelessness at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where the vessels are close to the wall. When the animals jump in a normal leap, they do not land on them. So there is not even a careless start here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for the 'liable' view by setting the ברייתא in a specific case where the owner was never careless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A jumping animal leaps out away from the wall. Vessels sitting right next to the wall could only be hit if the animal fell. Since the owner had no reason to fear a jump would hurt those vessels, the whole event is an accident from start to finish. So the ברייתא proves nothing about mixed cases.

keyTerms.meaning: For example; the case is one where…
Where the vessels are close to the wall

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is saying a careless start doesn't matter. It is saying that in this case there was no carelessness at all, because a normal jump could never have reached these vessels.

phrases.english: For example, where the vessels are close to the wall,
so that when they jump with a leap,
they do not land on them;
and there is not even a careless start.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the vessels were placed where only a fall could hit them
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was a mixed case of a careless start and an accidental end, and it ruled exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is a pure accident with no carelessness at all, so even the 'liable' view agrees it is exempt.

steps.title: רב זביד: sometimes even a fall makes the owner pay
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא says there are cases where the owner is liable even when the animals fell. This happens with a shaky wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: sometimes he is liable even when they fell. You find this with a shaky wall.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא adds a new rule. There are cases where a fall, not just a jump, makes the owner pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now a fall meant exempt. רב זביד says that when the wall is shaky, letting the animals up there is itself careless, so a fall can make the owner liable. The גמרא will next ask exactly why.

keyTerms.meaning: You can find it (such a case exists)

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
Sometimes, even if they fell, he is also liable.
You find it with a shaky wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the ברייתא's rule that animals who fell are exempt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An owner can be liable even when his animals fell, for example with a shaky wall.

steps.title: A shaky wall would still be an accident in the end
steps.stepSummary: If the carelessness was about bricks falling, then the bricks did not fall. The animals fell instead, so this is a careless start with an accidental end.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? That he should have thought the bricks might fall? In the end, the bricks did not fall. They fell. That is a careless start with an accidental end!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב זביד's shaky-wall example by asking what exactly made the owner careless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shaky wall makes you worry about its bricks falling. But the damage here came from the animals falling, which is a different thing. So the carelessness did not cause this damage. That is a mixed case, which this תנא exempts.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? (what is the reason?)
To think about it; to expect it
In the end; when all is said and done

phrases.english: What is the reason?
That he should have thought
that the bricks would fall?
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is the corrected wording, making the verb plural: 'the bricks fall.'

phrases.english: In the end, the bricks did not fall,
and they fell instead;
phrases.notes: 'They' means the dog and the goat.

phrases.english: it is a careless start with an accidental end!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי נִיהוּ דְּאִבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְאַסּוֹקֵי דַּעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the example given in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב זביד's example of a shaky wall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The danger of a shaky wall is falling bricks, but the damage came from the animals falling. That makes it a mixed case, which this תנא exempts.

steps.title: It means a narrow wall
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד was talking about a narrow wall, where the animals falling is exactly the danger one should expect.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for a narrow wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing the example from a shaky wall to a narrow wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On a narrow wall, the obvious danger is that the animals themselves will fall off. So the carelessness and the damage are the same thing, and the whole event counts as carelessness, not as a mixed case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for… (the ruling is talking about this case)

steps.whatToRemember: A fall makes the owner pay only when the fall itself was the danger he should have expected, like a narrow wall. A careless act that leads to a different, accidental kind of damage is exempt for this תנא.

phrases.english: It is needed only for a narrow wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16 by redefining רב זביד's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: a narrow wall instead of a shaky one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב זביד meant a shaky wall, where the danger was falling bricks.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב זביד means a narrow wall, where the animals falling is the very danger, so the owner was careless about exactly what happened.

steps.title: Jumping up versus jumping down
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a dog or goat that jumped upward makes its owner exempt, and one that jumped downward makes him liable. A person or a rooster is liable whichever way they jumped.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: a dog or a goat that leaped from below to above is exempt. From above to below, they are liable. A person or a rooster that leaped, whether from above to below or from below to above, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that sorts out jumping damage by direction and by who did the jumping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a dog or a goat, direction matters. Jumping down is their normal way, so the owner is liable, while jumping up gets an exemption. A person and a rooster are liable either way, so for them direction makes no difference.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A dog or a goat that leaped
from below to above: they are exempt.
From above to below: they are liable.
A person or a rooster that leaped:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מִלְּמַעְלָה לְמַטָּה, בֵּין מִלְּמַטָּה לְמַעְלָה – חַיָּיבִין.
phrases.english: whether from above to below or from below to above, they are liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא that adds the direction of the leap to the topic of jumping animals from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dog or goat leaping up: exempt. Leaping down: liable. A person or a rooster: liable in both directions.
